planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks after the last frost for a summer crop, or in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop. Unlike many heirloom Chioggia-type radicchios that need a hard freeze to redden and firm up, 'Indigo' reliably forms tight round heads without an extended cold period, making it one of the few radicchios suited to spring planting.

directions: This early-maturing F1 hybrid produces tight, softball-sized heads of glossy garnet-red leaves with crisp white ribs in as few as 55 to 65 days, making it one of the more dependable radicchios for gardeners outside the classic Italian growing regions. Unlike many open-pollinated Chioggia-type radicchios that need a hard freeze to redden and firm up, 'Indigo' forms well-blanched, uniformly colored heads even from a spring sowing, though a light fall frost still sweetens the flavor. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm to the touch, since they can split or bolt if left too long in warm weather. Its dependable heading habit and shorter cycle make it a good choice for succession planting through the growing season.

planting.note: Direct sow from just before the last frost through early summer for a warm-season crop, or in late summer for a fall crop. 'Fiero' colors up reliably without the cutback-and-regrow forcing technique that traditional Tardivo-type Treviso radicchio requires.

directions: This elongated, torpedo-shaped F1 hybrid resembles the classic heirloom Treviso radicchios but matures in a much shorter 50 to 60 days and colors reliably without the traditional post-cutback forcing that old-style Tardivo types need. Leaves are deep wine-red with prominent white midribs, held in slim, upright, self-blanching heads that stay tender as they size up. 'Fiero' tolerates a wider sowing window than most chicories, performing well from both an early sowing and a late-summer sowing for fall harvest. Its quicker cycle and forgiving nature make it a practical way to get Treviso's elegant shape without the long season or hands-on forcing older varieties require.

planting.note: Direct sow in late spring to early summer so roots can bulk up over the summer before fall harvest and forcing. As an F1 hybrid, 'Zoom' produces more uniform, evenly sized roots than many open-pollinated witloof strains, which improves the percentage of well-shaped chicons from a given planting.

directions: 'Zoom' is a widely grown F1 witloof chicory selected for producing homegrown Belgian endive, valued for uniform, blemish-free, torpedo-shaped roots that size up reliably even without the deep, stone-free soil older open-pollinated witloof strains prefer. Sow directly in late spring to early summer and grow through the season to develop a taproot roughly 1.5 to 2 inches across; in fall, cut the foliage back to an inch above the crown, lift the roots, and hold them cold until ready to force. To produce chicons, replant the trimmed roots upright and closely spaced in a deep container of moist sand or soil, cover completely to exclude all light, and hold at 50-60F; pale, tightly furled chicons are ready to cut in three to four weeks. Because the roots bulk up more evenly than many older varieties, this hybrid tends to give a higher yield of usable chicons per planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in late spring; this later-maturing forcing hybrid is best suited to growers who want a longer field season and roots that hold well in cold storage for staggered forcing batches deep into winter.

directions: 'Totem' is a later-maturing F1 witloof chicory bred for growers who want to stagger their Belgian endive harvest well into winter, since its roots hold in cold storage and continue to force well after several months. Direct sow in late spring and grow through summer to develop a thick, straight taproot; in fall, trim the foliage to an inch above the crown, lift the roots before hard freezes, and store them cold and dark until needed. Force a batch every few weeks by replanting roots upright in moist sand or soil in complete darkness at 50-60F, and expect compact, ivory-white chicons in three to four weeks. Compared to earlier-maturing forcing hybrids, its slightly longer field season produces larger roots that can support a second, smaller flush of growth if the first chicon is cut and the root is forced again.

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost for a spring-to-summer crop, or in late summer for the traditional fall crop. Improved bolt resistance lets 'Frenzy' be sown earlier in spring than older frisee-type endives, which tend to bolt if planted before day length starts to shorten.

directions: 'Frenzy' is a fast, uniform frisee-type endive with finely dissected, frizzy leaves and improved bolt resistance that lets it be direct sown in spring as well as in the late-summer window most curly endives need. Heads self-blanch as the deeply cut outer leaves arch over the pale, feathery heart, though tying the outer leaves closed for the last week or two before harvest produces a larger blanched center. Its quicker 45 to 55 day cycle and heat tolerance make it more forgiving of an early sowing than older frisee varieties. Harvest whole heads at the base once the centers are tight, or pick individual outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop while the heart keeps developing.
